parts.problem_md:
A yellow crystalline solid **E** dissolved in distilled water to give a yellow solution.

Addition of dilute sulfuric acid to this solution produced an orange solution **F**.

Warming **F** with ethanol resulted in a green solution **G**, and the formation of ethanol.

A standard cell was set up using solutions of **F** and **G** for the right-hand electrode and ethanol and ethanal for the left-hand electrode.

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> was found to be +1.94 V.

CH<sub>3</sub>CHO (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> $\rightleftharpoons$ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (aq)   *E*<sup>θ</sup> = –0.61 V

Deduce the formulae of the ions responsible for the colours of **F** and **G**, using the standard electrode potential and *E*<sup>θ</sup> given, and the values in the Data Booklet.
parts.solution_md:
To deduce the formulae of the ions responsible for the colours of **F** and **G**:

- Equation relating* E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> to half-cell values
**AND**
Determination of* E*<sup>θ</sup> for the right-hand electrode
*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>R</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>L</sub>
1.94 = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>R</sub> − (−0.61)
*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>R</sub> = 1.94 − 0.61= (+)1.33 (V); **[1 mark] **
- Identification of** F** and **G**
**F** = Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>
**AND**
**G** = Cr<sup>3+</sup>; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 2 marks] **

- *E*<sup>*θ*</sup><sub>*cell*</sub>* = **E*<sup>*θ*</sup><sub>*Right hand side*</sub>*  − **E*<sup>*θ*</sup><sub>*Left hand side *</sub>
- *Double-check the information from the data booklet as it is easy to use or identify the wrong one*
- *To gain the second mark you can give*

  - *(+)1.33 (V) with some working which relates 1.33 to 1.94 and −0.61*
  - *(+)1.33 (V) with the Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* / Cr*<sup>*3+*</sup>* half equation*
- *You need to use your knowledge of the oxidation of alcohols to help you answer this question*

  - *You know that acidified potassium dichromate turns from orange to green during this type of reaction*
  - *In the question, it tells you that F is the orange (Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>*) and G is green (Cr*<sup>*3+*</sup>*)*

parts.problem_md: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of the aqueous solution of **E** with dilute sulfuric acid. State symbols are not required.
parts.solution_md:
The ionic equation for the reaction of the aqueous solution of **E** with dilute sulfuric acid

- 2CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> ⇌ Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O;** [1 mark] **

- *You now know that Cr*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*7*</sub><sup>*2− *</sup>*(dichromate(VI) ion) is formed from the yellow crystalline solid **E** when added to sulfuric acid *

|   | **Electrode reaction** | `bold italic E to the power of bold ⦵`**/ V** |

| 6 | $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 3e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ MnO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | +1.70 |
| 7 | $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$+ 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ MnO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | +2.26 |

i) Write the ionic equation for the disproportionation of manganate(VI) ions, $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$, in **acidic** conditions, using relevant half-equations from the table. State symbols are not required.

**(2)**

ii) Calculate `E subscript cell superscript ⦵` for the disproportionation of manganate(VI) ions in **acidic **conditions, stating whether or not the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

**(2)**

iii) Using the standard electrode potentials in the table, assess the thermodynamic feasibility of preparing manganate(VI) by reacting manganate(VII) and manganese(IV) oxide in **alkaline** conditions.

**(4)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The ionic equation for the disproportionation of manganate(VI) ions, $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$, in **acidic** conditions is:

- Selection of the correct half-equations from the table:
[1] MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + e<sup>− </sup>⇌ MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>
**AND** [7] MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 4H<sup>+ </sup>+ 2e<sup>− </sup>⇌ MnO<sub>2 </sub>+ 2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**
- Writing the balanced equation:
3MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 4H<sup>+ </sup>⇌ 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + MnO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) Calculating `E subscript cell superscript ⦵` for the disproportionation of manganate(VI) ions in **acidic **condition and whether or not the reaction is thermodynamically feasible:

- `begin mathsize 14px style E subscript cell superscript ⦵ end style` = 2.26 − 0.56; **[1 mark]**
- = (+)1.70 (V)
**AND**
(Positive so reaction is) feasible; **[1 mark]**

iii) Assessing the thermodynamic feasibility of preparing manganate(VI) by reacting manganate(VII) and manganese(IV) oxide in **alkaline** conditions:

For marking points 1 and 2:    
**EITHER**

- 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + MnO<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>− </sup>⇌ 3MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**
- `begin mathsize 14px style E subscript cell superscript ⦵ end style` = 0.56 − 0.59 = -0.03 (V); **[1 mark]**
**OR**
- Clearly identifies half-equations 1 and 2 from the table; **[1 mark]**
- Use of the anticlockwise rule or similar to show that the required reaction is not favoured, e.g. desired reaction moves ‘clockwise’ so not (thermodynamically) feasible; **[1 mark]** 
**OR**
 `begin mathsize 14px style E subscript cell superscript ⦵ end style` = 0.56 − 0.59 = -0.03 (V); **[1 mark]**

**For marking points 3 and 4:**

- (-) 0.03 V / `begin mathsize 14px style E subscript cell superscript ⦵ end style`is (very) small 
**OR**
The equilibrium has significant concentrations of reactants and products; **[1 mark]**
- The reaction may be shifted in the required direction using concentrated alkali / increasing alkaline concentration; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *In part (i)*

  - *As it refers to the disproportionation of manganate(VI) ions, MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>*, the two half-equation selected need to both contain MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>
  - *Manganate(VI) ions need to both oxidise and reduce, this occurs in acidic conditions, so H+ ions also need to be present*
  - *So you need to select a half-equation containing MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2- *</sup>*and H*<sup>*+*</sup>* on the left-hand side that has a more positive electrode potential than a half-equation that has MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2- *</sup>*on the right-hand side. i.e. half-equations 1 and 7*
  - *As equation 7 has the more positive electrode potential, the forward reaction will occur and manganate(VI) ions are reduced:*
  
    - *MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* + 4H*<sup>*+ *</sup>*+ 2e*<sup>*− *</sup>*⇌ MnO*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *As equation 1 has the less positive electrode potential, the reverse reaction will occur and manganate(VI) ions are oxidised:*
  
    - *MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2−  *</sup>*⇌ MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*−*</sup>* + e*<sup>*−*</sup>
  - *If you gave the correct but unbalanced ionic equation, you would score 1 mark*
  
    - *Remember**: To balance, when combining the two half-equations, the number of electrons needs to be the same, so multiply the equations as necessary to ensure the electrons are equal*
    - *In this case, multiply the reverse of equation 1 by 2 before combining*
  - *You would have been awarded the 2 marks if you had selected equations 1 and 5 and given the full balanced equation as:*
  
    - *5MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* + 8H*<sup>*+ *</sup>*⇌ 4MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*−*</sup>* + Mn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* + 4H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Use of alkaline half-equations to give 3MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2−*</sup>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O ⇌ 2MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*−*</sup>* + MnO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 4OH*<sup>*−*</sup>* scores 1 mark*
- *In part (ii)*

  - `E subscript cell superscript ⦵ space equals space E subscript reduction superscript ⦵ space minus space E subscript oxidation superscript ⦵`* = +2.26 - (+0.56) = +1.70 V*
  - *You would gain these two marks if:*
  
    - *You used equations 1 and 5 and gave *`E subscript cell superscript ⦵`* = +1.51 - (+0.56) = +0.95 V and stated that the reaction was feasible*
    - *You used the alkaline half-equations and gave *`E subscript cell superscript ⦵`* = +0.59 − (+)0.56 = +0.03 V and stated that the reaction was feasible*
  - *You would gain one mark for a correct value for the cell potential, without a comment on the feasibility*
- *In part (iii)*

  - *Half-equations 1 and 2 are the appropriate equations to select as they include all the necessary ions and OH*<sup>*-*</sup>* ions needed for alkaline conditions*
  - *In order to prepare manganate(VI) ions, the forward reaction of equation 1 and the reverse of equation 2 needs to occur*
  - *This is not thermodynamically feasible as this would give a negative cell potential*
  - *By increasing the concentration of OH*<sup>*-*</sup>* ions, the reverse reaction in equation 2 is favoured, causing its electrode potential to become less positive*
  - *This would then cause the cell potential to become positive and therefore feasible*

parts.problem_md:
Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. A group of students determined the iron content of a sample of steel wire by a titration method.

A known mass of the wire was dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and the resulting solution made up to 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> with more dilute sulfuric acid and mixed thoroughly.

Fe + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → FeSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>

25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> samples of the resulting solution were titrated with 0.0195 mol dm<sup>−3 </sup>potassium manganate(VII) solution.

i) State the colour change at the end-point of the titration.

**(1)**

ii) One student used 1.53 g of the wire (weighed directly on the balance pan) and obtained a mean titre of 27.35 cm<sup>3</sup> .

Using half-equations 3 and 5 from the table, calculate the percentage of iron in the steel wire. Give your answer to **three** significant figures.

**(5)**

iii) A second student carried out the same experiment but used distilled water to make up the solution in the volumetric flask.
A brown suspension formed during the titration. Explain how, if at all, the titre value would be affected by this student’s error.

**(3)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The colour change at the end-point of the titration is:

- Colourless
**AND**
To pale pink; **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage of iron in the steel wire is:

- **Calculation of moles of manganate(VII) in 27.35 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**:** 27.35 x 0.0195 x 10<sup>−3 </sup> = 5.33325 x 10<sup>−4</sup> / 0.000533325 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- **Use of 1:5 ratio to calculate mol Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** in 25.0 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**:** 5 x 5.33325 x 10<sup>−4</sup> = 2.666625 x 10<sup>−3</sup> / 0.002666625 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- **Scaling to 250.0 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** to give mol Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** in 250.0 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**:** 10 x 2.666625 x 10<sup>−3</sup> = 2.666625 x 10<sup>−2</sup> / 0.02666625 mol); **[1 mark]**
- **Conversion of mol to g of iron**:  2.666625 x 10<sup>−2</sup> x 55.8 = 1.48798 (g); **[1 mark]**
- **Calculation of percentage of iron in the wire:** $\frac{1.48798}{1.53}\times100$ = 97.25338 **AND** **Give the final value to 3 SF:** = 97.3%; **[1 mark]**

iii) The titre value would be affected by the student’s error by:

- The brown suspension formed is manganese(IV) oxide / MnO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Mn(VII) to Mn(II) provides 5 electrons per MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> but Mn(VII) to Mn(IV) only provides 3 electrons; **[1 mark]**
- So more MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is needed / titre is greater; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 9 marks]**

- *The titration involves titrating a solution of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* against manganate(VII) ions*
- *A solution of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* may appear pale green, and this would be accepted instead of colourless (not just green)*
- *The end point is when the Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* have all reacted and a pale tinge appears due to the excess manganate(VII) ions*

  - *Careful**: Despite the purple / magenta colour of a solution of manganate(VII), this is not accepted as the colour change, as this would mean too much manganate(VII) solution had been added and the end point would have been surpassed*
- *When performing these types of redox titration calculations, as with any titration calculations, you must use the molar ratios to help calculate the number of moles of each reactant*

  - *Careful**: Only 25.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of the original 250 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* solution is used in the titration, therefore in the original 250 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* solution, there would have been 10 times the number of Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* moles that there were in the 25.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* solution used in the titration*
- *In part (iii), as the solution is made up of distilled water as opposed to sulfuric acid, equation 6 occurs instead of equation 5 as fewer hydrogen ions are present, producing MnO2 which is the brown precipitate*

  - *The full ionic equation for the reaction with Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* ions is:*
  
    - *MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* + 4H*<sup>*+*</sup>* + 3Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* → MnO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 3Fe*<sup>*3+*</sup>
  - *Compared with the full ionic equation for the formation of Mn2+:*
  
    - *MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* + 5H*<sup>*+*</sup>* + 5Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* → Mn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* + 4H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 5Fe*<sup>*3+*</sup>
  - *This means that more MnO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*-*</sup>* is required to react with Fe*<sup>*2+*</sup>* when MnO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is produced*
  - *For the second marking point, you could explain in terms of oxidation numbers*
  - *If no other mark is scored, one mark is allowed for the titration is no longer quantitative as another reaction is (also) taking place*

parts.problem_md:
Some standard electrode potentials are shown below.

| Half-equation | *E*° / V |
|---|---|
| Ce<sup>4+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ce<sup>3+</sup> (aq) | +1.70 |
| VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ VO<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | +1.00 |

These two half-cells are connected to form an electrochemical cell using the apparatus shown.

![A line drawing of an electrochemical cell. Two beakers are connected by a salt bridge: the left contains (VO2)+ (aq) and (VO)2+ (aq) in H2SO4 (aq); the right contains Ce4+ (aq) and Ce3+ (aq). Each beaker has a platinum electrode connected to a voltmeter via an external circuit.](assets/005-a-line-drawing-of-an-electrochemical-cell-two-be.png)

State which species is oxidised in this cell.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species oxidised in this cell is:
> 
> - Vanadium(IV) ions / VO<sup>2+</sup>
> **OR**
> Vanadium in the +4 oxidation state **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The species with the less positive *E*° value gets oxidised, acting as the reducing agent:
> 
> - VO<sup>2+</sup> at +1.00 V is oxidised at the anode.
> - Ce<sup>4+</sup> at +1.70 V is reduced at the cathode.
> 
> A quick rule: the species on the left-hand side of the more positive half-equation is always the oxidising agent.

parts.problem_md: Write the half-equation for the reaction occurring at the negative electrode of this cell.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode is:
> 
> - VO<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept equilibrium arrows.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The negative electrode is the anode, where oxidation occurs. Write the VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>/VO<sup>2+</sup> half-equation in the forward direction (as oxidation, not reduction).
> 
> H<sub>2</sub>O and H<sup>+</sup> must both be included and correctly balanced. Omitting either one loses the mark.

parts.problem_md: Calculate the standard cell potential, *E*°<sub>cell</sub>, for this cell.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the standard cell potential:

- Identify the reduction and oxidation half-cells:

  - Cathode (Ce<sup>4+</sup>/Ce<sup>3+</sup>): *E*° = +1.70 V
  - Anode (VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>/VO<sup>2+</sup>): *E*° = +1.00 V
- Apply the equation:

*E*°<sub>cell</sub> = *E*°<sub>cathode</sub> − *E*°<sub>anode</sub>

*E*°<sub>cell</sub> = (+1.70) - (+1.00)

*E*°<sub>cell</sub> = **+0.70 V ****[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always use *E*°<sub>cell</sub> = *E*°<sub>cathode</sub> − *E*°<sub>anode</sub> (both as reduction potentials). Do not add the two values.
> 
> A positive *E*°<sub>cell</sub> confirms the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

parts.problem_md: Write the overall ionic equation for the reaction occurring in this cell.
parts.solution_md:
To write the overall ionic equation:

- Write the reduction equation:

Ce<sup>4+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ce<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

- Reverse the other equation for oxidation:

VO<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>-</sup>

- Combine the equations:

  - Balance for H<sup>+</sup> (aq), H<sub>2</sub>O and e<sup>-</sup> if necessary

Ce<sup>4+</sup> (aq) + VO<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Ce<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products (Ce<sup>4+</sup>, VO<sup>2+</sup>, Ce<sup>3+</sup>, VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing, including 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) and H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not cancel or omit H<sub>2</sub>O or H<sup>+</sup> from the equation. Both are genuine products/reactants and their absence loses the balancing mark.

parts.problem_md: Both half-cells require platinum electrodes. Explain why.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Platinum electrodes are needed because:
> 
> - All species in both half-cells are ions in solution / there is no solid metal present to act as an electrode **[1 mark]**
> - Platinum is an inert electrical conductor that does not react with any species in either half-cell
> **OR**
> Platinum conducts electrons without participating in or interfering with the cell reactions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A metal electrode (for example, a zinc rod) is used when the metal itself appears in the half-equation (for example, Zn<sup>2+</sup>/Zn).
> 
> When both species are aqueous ions with no solid metal present, an inert electrode is needed to make electrical contact.
> 
> Platinum and graphite are both acceptable inert electrode materials.

parts.problem_md: State the purpose of the salt bridge in this cell.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The purpose of the salt bridge is to:
> 
> - Allow ions to flow between the two half-cell solutions / complete the circuit by allowing ion migration **[1 mark]**
> - Maintain electrical neutrality in each half-cell / prevent charge build-up that would stop current flowing **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons. Electrons flow through the external wire from the anode to the cathode.
> 
> Without the salt bridge, charge would accumulate in each half-cell (one becoming positive, one negative) and the cell would quickly stop working.

parts.problem_md: Which of these is the correctly balanced half-equation for the reduction of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) to Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) in acidic solution?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Write the unbalanced half-equation:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup>

- Balance Mn:

  - One manganese atom on each side
  - Already balanced

- Balance O:

  - Add 4H<sub>2</sub>O to the right-hand side:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + **4H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**

- Balance H:

  - Add 8H<sup>+</sup> to the left-hand side:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + **8H**<sup>**+**</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

- Balance charge:

  - Left side = (−1) + (+8) = +7
  - Right side = +2
  - Add 5e<sup>-</sup> to the left to balance:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + **5e**<sup>**-**</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

**A** is incorrect as using 4H<sup>+</sup> and 2H<sub>2</sub>O does not account for all four oxygen atoms in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>. 4H<sub>2</sub>O requires 8H<sup>+</sup>, not 4H<sup>+</sup>

**C** is incorrect as the mass balance is correct (8H<sup>+</sup>, 4H<sub>2</sub>O), but the electron count is wrong. The left-hand side has a net charge of +7 and the right-hand side is +2, so 5 electrons are needed, not 7

**D** is incorrect as the values 14H<sup>+</sup> and 7H<sub>2</sub>O belong to the dichromate(VI) half-equation (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> + **14H**<sup>**+**</sup> + 6e<sup>-</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + **7H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**), not manganate(VII). MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> has only four oxygen atoms, requiring 4H<sub>2</sub>O and 8H<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not try to recall the numbers in this half-equation from memory.
> 
> If you learn to derive it from scratch (balance O first with H<sub>2</sub>O, then H with H<sup>+</sup>, then charge with e<sup>-</sup>), you will always get it right.
> 
> This method works for any redox half-equation and is far more reliable than rote recall under exam conditions.

parts.problem_md: Which half-equation correctly represents the reaction occurring at the anode of an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- At the anode, oxidation occurs

  - H<sub>2</sub> loses electrons
- In alkaline conditions, OH<sup>-</sup> ions are present and water is the product
- Write the unbalanced half-equation:

H<sub>2</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>O

- Balance H:

  - Add 2OH<sup>-</sup> to the left:

H<sub>2</sub> + **2OH**<sup>**-**</sup> → **2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**

- Balance charge:

  - Left side = −2
  - Right side = 0
  - Add 2e<sup>-</sup> to the right:

H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>-</sup> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + **2e**<sup>**-**</sup>

**B** is incorrect as this is the cathode half-equation where O<sub>2</sub> is reduced. The cathode is where reduction occurs, not the anode.

**C** is incorrect as this is the anode equation for an acidic fuel cell, not an alkaline one. In alkaline conditions H<sup>+</sup> ions are not available and OH<sup>-</sup> is the relevant species.

**D** is incorrect as this is the cathode equation for an acidic fuel cell. It uses H<sup>+</sup> ions, which are not present at significant concentration in alkaline conditions.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error is confusing the anode and cathode reactions. Remember:
> 
> - Anode = oxidation (hydrogen loses electrons)
> - Cathode = reduction (oxygen gains electrons).
> 
> In alkaline conditions, always include OH<sup>-</sup> in the anode equation as H<sub>2</sub> reacts with hydroxide ions, not H<sup>+</sup>. If the question specifies alkaline, any equation with H<sup>+</sup> is automatically wrong.
